blocks.text: Boiler corrosion is deterioration of boiler metal due to chemical or electrochemical attack by impurities in water.

blocks.title: Causes and control
items: Dissolved oxygen causes pitting. Remove it by deaeration and suitable oxygen scavengers such as sodium sulphite.
CO₂ dissolves to form carbonic acid, attacking metal, especially condensate lines. Remove dissolved gases and control water chemistry.
MgCl₂ can hydrolyse under boiler conditions to produce acidic conditions; remove such salts by proper feedwater treatment.

blocks.text: Prevention combines external water treatment, deaeration, monitored alkalinity/pH and suitable conditioning.

blocks.title: Treatment sequence
items: Screening: pass raw water through screens to remove leaves, sticks and other large floating matter.
Coagulation and flocculation: add a suitable coagulant such as alum; gelatinous Al(OH)₃ traps fine suspended/colloidal impurities in larger flocs.
Sedimentation: allow the flocs and suspended solids to settle; withdraw the clarified water.
Filtration: pass it through a sand/gravel bed to remove remaining suspended material and reduce microorganisms.
Disinfection: chlorinate or use another suitable process to destroy pathogens; provide a controlled residual for distribution.

blocks.text: A sand filter contains fine sand above coarser sand and supporting gravel, with an under-drain to collect filtered water. Retained particles and the surface layer improve filtration. Slow filters are cleaned by removing the clogged surface sand; rapid filters are cleaned by backwashing. Filtration reduces microbial loading, but disinfection is still needed.

HOCl provides the main disinfecting action. Store and distribute the treated water hygienically and check its microbial and chemical quality. Ordinary sand filtration does not remove all dissolved salts; add specific treatment where raw-water quality requires it.
Demineralisation removes both cations and anions by passing water through a cation exchanger in H⁺ form and an anion exchanger in OH⁻ form.

blocks.title: Process
items: Cation column: acidic resin RH exchanges H⁺ for dissolved Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ and other cations. The effluent contains the corresponding acids.
Anion column: basic resin R′OH exchanges OH⁻ for Cl⁻, SO₄²⁻ and other anions.
The released H⁺ and OH⁻ combine to form water, producing water of very low ionic content.

blocks.text: Principle: at pH about 10, EDTA forms stable 1:1 complexes with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺. Eriochrome Black T (EBT) forms a wine-red metal–indicator complex. EDTA binds the metal ions more strongly and releases the blue indicator at the end point.

blocks.title: Procedure
items: Standardise the EDTA solution using a known standard hard-water sample, with NH₄Cl–NH₄OH buffer at pH 10 and EBT.
Pipette a measured volume of the water sample into a conical flask. Add buffer and a few drops of EBT; the solution becomes wine-red.
Titrate with standardised EDTA until the colour changes from wine-red to clear blue. Record the EDTA volume.
For permanent hardness, boil another measured sample, cool, filter and wash the precipitate, and make the filtrate back to the original volume. Titrate an equal aliquot as above.
Temporary hardness = total hardness − permanent hardness.

blocks.text: Galvanic corrosion occurs when two dissimilar metals are electrically connected in an electrolyte. The more active metal becomes the anode and dissolves; the more noble metal acts as the cathode.
Example: an iron screw in a copper fitting. In aerated neutral water, the reactions are:
Electrons flow through the metallic connection from iron to copper; ionic movement in the electrolyte completes the circuit. Attack is severe for a small anode coupled to a large cathode.

blocks.title: Prevention
items: Use the same metal or metals close in the galvanic series.
Electrically insulate dissimilar-metal joints and keep them dry.
Avoid a small anodic area connected to a large cathodic area; use suitable coatings/protection.

blocks.text: Differential-aeration corrosion occurs when different regions of the same metal contact an electrolyte with unequal oxygen concentrations. The oxygen-poor region is anodic and corrodes; the oxygen-rich region is cathodic.
Example: in a partly filled steel tank, the region just below the waterline has less oxygen than the surface region and is attacked.

blocks.text: Wet or electrochemical corrosion occurs when a metal contacts moisture or an electrolyte. Anodic and cathodic regions develop on the surface. Metal dissolves at the anode, electrons travel through the metal, and reduction occurs at the cathode.

Small surface differences, impurities or unequal oxygen concentration establish local electrochemical cells. An electrical path through the metal and an ionic path through the electrolyte complete the circuit. Only the anodic areas lose iron directly.
Hydrogen-evolution mechanism: in an acidic, poorly aerated medium, hydrogen ions accept electrons at the cathode.

Hydrogen ions are consumed at the cathode and hydrogen bubbles escape, while ferrous ions enter the solution at the anode. The cathodic process is therefore hydrogen evolution rather than rust formation itself.
Oxygen-absorption mechanism: in aerated neutral or alkaline water, dissolved oxygen accepts electrons at cathodic regions.

The oxygen-poor region usually acts as the anode, while the better-aerated region supports oxygen reduction. Ferrous ions and hydroxide ions meet in the electrolyte to form ferrous hydroxide, which is further oxidised in the presence of oxygen and water.
Ferric hydroxide undergoes dehydration and ageing to form hydrated ferric oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O (rust). Rust is porous and non-protective, allowing corrosion to continue.

Hydrogen ions are consumed at the cathode and hydrogen bubbles escape, while ferrous ions enter the solution at the anode. The cathodic process is therefore hydrogen evolution rather than rust formation itself.
Oxygen-absorption mechanism: in aerated neutral or alkaline water, dissolved oxygen accepts electrons at cathodic regions.

The oxygen-poor region usually acts as the anode, while the better-aerated region supports oxygen reduction. Ferrous ions and hydroxide ions meet in the electrolyte to form ferrous hydroxide, which is further oxidised in the presence of oxygen and water.
Ferric hydroxide undergoes dehydration and ageing to form hydrated ferric oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O (rust). Rust is porous and non-protective, allowing corrosion to continue.

Rust is porous and non-protective, so oxygen and moisture continue to reach the metal. Unequal oxygen access, dissolved salts and small anodic regions promote local attack. The coupled oxidation and reduction reactions explain why both an electrolyte and a cathodic reaction are necessary for wet corrosion.

Corrosion is the deterioration of a metal by chemical or electrochemical reaction with its environment. Dry corrosion is direct chemical attack by gases, commonly oxygen, without a bulk aqueous electrolyte, often at high temperature.

blocks.title: Oxidation mechanism
items: Oxygen adsorbs on the metal surface and reacts to form an oxide film.
Metal atoms lose electrons to form metal ions; oxygen gains electrons to form oxide ions.
Further oxidation requires outward diffusion of metal ions or inward diffusion of oxygen species through the film.
Oxide-film continuity, adhesion and permeability therefore control continued attack.

blocks.text: Conducting polymers conduct electricity through their conjugated backbone or incorporated conducting materials.

Vehicles, phones, backup and energy storage.

blocks.text: During discharge both convert chemical energy to electrical energy by oxidation at the anode and reduction at the cathode. In secondary batteries, charging restores the active materials; cycle life is finite.
A methanol–oxygen fuel cell converts the chemical energy of methanol and oxygen directly into electrical energy.
Construction: two catalytic electrodes are separated by a proton-exchange membrane such as Nafion. The anode contains platinum–ruthenium catalyst and the cathode contains platinum catalyst.

blocks.title: Working
items: Aqueous methanol is supplied to the anode, where it is oxidised to carbon dioxide, protons and electrons.
Protons pass through the membrane to the cathode.
Electrons pass through the external circuit and produce current.
Oxygen supplied to the cathode combines with protons and electrons to form water.

blocks.text: The membrane conducts protons but does not provide the external electron path. Continuous supply of methanol and oxygen maintains operation, while carbon dioxide and water are removed. The fuel cell therefore produces electricity directly without first converting the fuel energy into mechanical work.
A PEM fuel cell converts continuously supplied hydrogen and oxygen into electricity using a proton-exchange membrane.

blocks.title: Construction and working
items: Two porous catalytic gas-diffusion electrodes lie on opposite sides of a proton-conducting polymer membrane, such as Nafion.
Hydrogen enters the anode and oxygen/air enters the cathode. Flow channels/current collectors distribute gases and collect current.
At the anode, H₂ is oxidised. H⁺ crosses the membrane; electrons pass through the external load.
At the cathode, oxygen combines with H⁺ and electrons to form water. Remove water and heat and maintain membrane hydration.

blocks.text: Applications: fuel-cell vehicles, portable power, backup power and suitable stationary power systems. The membrane separates the gases and conducts protons while blocking electron flow.
Syngas (synthesis gas) is a mixture mainly of carbon monoxide and hydrogen. Fischer–Tropsch synthesis converts purified syngas into liquid hydrocarbons over a cobalt- or iron-based catalyst.

blocks.title: Process
items: Produce syngas, for example by passing steam over red-hot coke: C + H₂O → CO + H₂.
Remove sulphur compounds and adjust the H₂:CO ratio.
Compress the purified gas and pass it through the catalytic converter at about 200–300°C and 5–25 atm in the course process.
Cool the products, separate liquids and fractionate them into fuel fractions; recycle suitable unreacted gas.

blocks.text: The course catalyst contains Co with thoria/magnesia promoters on kieselguhr support. The process makes liquid fuels from feedstocks such as coal, natural gas or biomass instead of relying only on crude petroleum.

rows: LPG
Mainly propane and butane.
Liquefied under moderate pressure; convenient storage, high calorific value; heavier than air.
Cooking, heating and suitable vehicle fuel.
CNG
Mainly methane, stored as compressed gas.
High octane quality; lighter than air; lower particulate emissions than many conventional fuels.
Cars, buses and industrial/domestic fuel.
Hythane
Hydrogen blended with natural gas, commonly about 20% H₂ and 80% natural gas by volume in the course example.
Hydrogen can improve flame propagation and extend lean combustion; needs compatible storage/engine control.
Suitable modified gas-fuel engines and transport trials.

blocks.text: These are gaseous fuels with relatively clean combustion, but carbon-containing fuels still emit CO₂. Actual Hythane composition and emissions depend on the blend and operating conditions.
Green hydrogen is hydrogen produced by electrolysis of water using electricity from renewable sources such as solar and wind energy.
Construction: a proton-exchange membrane separates the anode and cathode. Water is supplied to the anode, and the electrodes are connected to a renewable-powered DC supply.

blocks.title: Working
items: At the positive anode, water splits into oxygen, hydrogen ions and electrons.
Hydrogen ions pass through the membrane to the negative cathode.
The external DC circuit supplies electrons to the cathode, where hydrogen gas is formed.

blocks.text: The solid polymer membrane conducts protons and keeps the product gases separated. PEM electrolysers give high-purity hydrogen and use catalytic electrodes. The electricity must come from renewable sources for the hydrogen to be called green.
Proximate analysis determines the mass percentages of moisture, volatile matter, ash and fixed carbon in coal.

rows: Moisture
Heat a known finely powdered sample at 105–110°C to constant mass; cool in a desiccator and weigh.
Moisture wastes heat on evaporation and increases transport/handling cost.
Volatile matter
Heat the dried sample in a covered crucible at about 925°C for 7 minutes, excluding air; weigh the additional loss.
Controls ignition, flame length, smoke and furnace/air-supply requirements.
Ash
Burn a known sample in an open crucible at about 700–750°C to constant residue.
Ash lowers useful heating value, causes slagging/clinkers and disposal problems.
Fixed carbon
Calculate by difference on the same reporting basis.
Indicates sustained solid-fuel burning and is important in coke and furnace design.

blocks.title: Volatile matter
blocks.latex: \%VM=\dfrac{\text{additional loss from dried sample}}{\text{original sample mass}}\times100

blocks.text: The reported values must use one consistent basis. Fixed carbon is not identical to total elemental carbon. The analysis helps grade coal, compare its suitability and design combustion equipment.
Ultimate analysis determines the percentages of carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, sulphur and oxygen in coal. It supports fuel-quality assessment, combustion-air calculations and pollution control.

blocks.title: Carbon and hydrogen
items: Burn a known mass m of coal completely in oxygen. Carbon forms CO₂ and hydrogen forms H₂O.
Pass products through weighed anhydrous CaCl₂ and KOH absorbers: CaCl₂ gains the water mass and KOH gains the CO₂ mass.

blocks.text: Nitrogen: in the Kjeldahl method, digest coal with concentrated H₂SO₄ and suitable catalyst/salts to convert nitrogen to ammonium sulphate. Add excess NaOH, distil NH₃ into standard acid and back-titrate the unused acid with a blank correction.
Here V is net mL of acid of normality N consumed by NH₃, and m is coal mass in grams.
Sulphur: burn coal in oxygen in a bomb, extract the sulphate and precipitate it with BaCl₂. Filter, wash, dry and weigh BaSO₄.
Oxygen is calculated by difference: on a dry basis, %O = 100 − (%C + %H + %N + %S + %ash). On an as-received basis, also subtract moisture. For an ash-free dry basis, subtract CHNS only.

rows: C and H
Main combustible constituents; influence heating value.
N
Little useful heat; contributes to NOₓ emissions.
S
Forms SOₓ, causing pollution and corrosion.
O
Already-combined oxygen generally reduces useful fuel heating value.

blocks.text: Catalytic cracking breaks heavy oil molecules into smaller, more useful hydrocarbons using a catalyst. In this circulating fluidised-bed process, finely powdered catalyst is carried continuously between a reactor and regenerator.

blocks.title: Working
items: Preheat the heavy oil, vaporise it and mix it with hot silica–alumina catalyst.
Pass the mixture into the reactor; cracking produces lighter hydrocarbons.
Cyclones separate catalyst particles from product vapours. Send vapours to the fractionating column and stabiliser to obtain gasoline and other fractions.
Coke deposits on the catalyst and reduces its activity. Send spent catalyst to the regenerator.
Burn off coke with air at about 600°C; return the hot regenerated catalyst to mix with fresh feed.

blocks.text: Continuous catalyst regeneration maintains activity, improves throughput and transfers heat to the cracking stage. Catalytic cracking produces better-quality petrol than simple thermal cracking under suitable conditions.
Lithium-ion batteries are preferred in electric vehicles because they combine high gravimetric/volumetric energy density with rechargeability.

blocks.title: Advantages
items: Store substantial energy with less battery mass, supporting vehicle range.
Give high cell voltage and efficient charge/discharge operation.
Have low self-discharge and useful cycle life with proper management.
Can supply the power required for acceleration and accept charging, including regenerative braking.

blocks.text: Their limitations include cost, thermal-runaway risk and ageing; a battery-management system controls voltage, temperature and charging. These controls are essential to obtaining the advantages safely.
Principle: methylene blue absorbs visible light. Within the working range, absorbance follows Beer–Lambert law.

blocks.title: Procedure
items: Prepare methylene-blue standards of known concentrations.
Set the instrument at the absorption maximum, approximately 664 nm in dilute aqueous solution.
Use a solvent blank and measure the absorbance of each standard.
Plot absorbance against concentration to obtain a calibration graph.
Measure the effluent sample under the same conditions.
Read its concentration from the calibration graph and apply any dilution factor.

blocks.text: In A = εlc, ε is molar absorptivity, l is the optical path length and c is concentration. Use the same cuvette and conditions for standards and sample. Dilute samples outside the calibration range; turbidity and other absorbing substances can interfere.
UV–Visible spectroscopy is therefore useful for measuring dye concentration and treatment efficiency.
Infrared spectroscopy detects molecular vibrations that absorb characteristic IR wavelengths.

blocks.title: Night-vision security
items: Warm objects emit infrared radiation. A passive thermal detector records differences in emitted radiation and converts them into an image.
This allows people or intruders to be detected in darkness. Active near-IR systems instead illuminate the scene and detect reflected IR.

blocks.title: CO pollution monitoring
items: CO absorbs infrared radiation near its characteristic band, about 4.6–4.7 μm.
In a non-dispersive IR analyser, an IR source sends radiation through a gas sample cell. A selected-band detector measures the decrease in transmitted intensity.
A reference channel and calibration relate absorption to CO concentration, allowing exhaust or workplace-air monitoring.

blocks.text: Diagram unavailable: the supplied notes do not provide a verified CO-analyser apparatus drawing. The analyser described here uses its own IR source; it is active IR absorption measurement.
Principle: STM works on quantum tunnelling of electrons between a sharp conducting tip and a conducting sample.

blocks.title: Working
items: Bring the tip very close to the sample and apply a small bias to produce a tunnelling current.
Move the tip across the surface using a piezoelectric scanner.
In constant-current mode, feedback adjusts the tip height to maintain constant current.
Record the height changes to obtain a surface image.

blocks.text: The main components are a sharp conducting tip, bias supply, piezoelectric scanner, current detector, feedback controller and computer. Tunnelling current changes very strongly with tip–sample separation, making small surface-height differences detectable. Constant-height mode instead records current changes while scanning at a fixed nominal tip height.
Uses: studying surface atoms, defects and nanostructures. The sample must provide a conducting path.
Applications also include atomic-scale study of conducting/semiconducting surfaces, adsorbed molecules, surface defects and manipulation of individual atoms under suitable conditions.
Self-healing materials possess a built-in ability to repair damage and restore their performance.

blocks.title: Working principle
items: Triggering: damage activates the healing mechanism.
Transportation: healing material moves into the damaged region.
Chemical repair: polymerisation or bond re-formation closes the crack.

blocks.text: In a microcapsule system, a crack breaks embedded capsules. The healing agent flows into the crack and reacts to form a solid repair. In intrinsic systems, reversible bonds reconnect, often with heating.

Capsule-based and vascular systems are extrinsic: healing material is stored in capsules or channels within the matrix. In intrinsic systems, repair arises from reversible bonds or interactions in the polymer itself. Healing can be autonomic, triggered by damage, or activated externally by heat or another stimulus.
Examples: protective coatings, polymer composites, concrete and scratch-repair coatings.
Self-healing materials repair damage through built-in healing mechanisms, helping restore function and extend service life.

rows: Protective coatings
Repair scratches/cracks to restore the corrosion barrier.
Aerospace and automotive composites
Repair microcracks to improve durability and reduce maintenance.
Construction
Self-healing concrete seals small cracks and reduces water ingress.
Electronics
Repair damage in suitable encapsulants or conductive components.
Consumer products
Scratch-repair polymer surfaces and durable finishes.

blocks.text: Capsule systems release a healing agent when cracked; intrinsic systems restore reversible bonds, often with heat. Performance depends on crack size, healing conditions and whether the healing agent can be replenished.
A biosensor combines a biological recognition element, such as an enzyme, with a transducer and signal-processing/display system.

blocks.title: Characteristics
items: Selectivity: distinguishes the target analyte using a suitable bioreceptor.
Sensitivity: detects small concentration changes in the working range.
Fast response and suitable recovery time.
Reproducibility and stability during storage and use.
Small sample requirement, simple operation and reliable calibration.

blocks.text: For example, immobilised glucose oxidase provides selectivity in an amperometric glucose sensor; the electrode converts the reaction into a measurable current. Interfering chemicals and changes in temperature/pH must be controlled.

rows: Approach
Reduces bulk material to nanoscale structures.
Builds structures from atoms, molecules or clusters.
Methods
Ball milling, etching and lithography.
Sol–gel, precipitation, self-assembly and chemical vapour deposition.
Control
Patterning is useful, but size distribution/defects may be concerns.
Nucleation and growth must be controlled to avoid aggregation.
Limitations
Can introduce surface defects or contamination.
Sensitive to reaction conditions and particle growth.

blocks.text: Nanomaterials have at least one dimension approximately 1–100 nm. High surface-to-volume ratio and size-dependent properties distinguish them from bulk materials.

rows: Approach
Reduces bulk material to nanoscale structures.
Builds structures from atoms, molecules or clusters.
Methods
Ball milling, etching and lithography.
Sol–gel, precipitation, self-assembly and chemical vapour deposition.
Control
Patterning is useful, but size distribution/defects may be concerns.
Nucleation and growth must be controlled to avoid aggregation.
Limitations
Can introduce surface defects or contamination.
Sensitive to reaction conditions and particle growth.

blocks.text: Top-down example—ball milling: repeated impact fractures bulk powder into fine particles. Bottom-up example—sol–gel: precursor hydrolysis and condensation form a sol and then a gel; controlled drying/heat treatment gives fine oxide material.
Lubricants reduce friction and wear by separating or protecting moving surfaces.

rows: Liquid
Mineral oils, vegetable/animal oils and synthetic oils such as silicones or esters.
Semi-solid
Greases: lubricating oil thickened with soap or another thickener; calcium, sodium and lithium greases.
Solid
Graphite, MoS₂ and PTFE, used where suitable liquid lubrication is difficult.
Emulsion
Oil–water systems, commonly used for combined cooling and lubrication in metalworking.

blocks.text: Selection depends on load, speed, temperature, environment and compatibility. Liquid oils can circulate and remove heat; greases stay in place; suitable solids serve severe or specialised environments.
Lubricants reduce friction and wear by separating or protecting moving surfaces.

rows: Liquid
Mineral oils, vegetable/animal oils and synthetic oils such as silicones or esters.
Semi-solid
Greases: lubricating oil thickened with soap or another thickener; calcium, sodium and lithium greases.
Solid
Graphite, MoS₂ and PTFE, used where suitable liquid lubrication is difficult.
Emulsion
Oil–water systems, commonly used for combined cooling and lubrication in metalworking.

blocks.text: Selection depends on load, speed, temperature, environment and compatibility. Liquid oils can circulate and remove heat; greases stay in place; suitable solids serve severe or specialised environments.

Extreme-pressure lubrication is required where heavy loads and high sliding/contact temperatures destroy ordinary oil or boundary films, for example in hypoid gears and severe metal-forming operations.

blocks.title: Mechanism
items: Add suitable sulphur-, phosphorus- or other reactive EP additives to the base oil.
At hot contact spots, additives react with the metal to form protective compounds such as sulphide/phosphate films.
These sacrificial, relatively low-shear films prevent direct metal contact, local welding and seizure.
As the film wears, fresh additive can react to restore protection.

blocks.text: The formulation must suit the metal and service conditions: reactive sulphur compounds may attack copper alloys. EP lubrication is a chemically formed protective film, not simply a thicker oil layer.

rows: Flash point
Lowest specified-test temperature at which vapour ignites momentarily.
Indicates volatility and fire risk; a low value may suggest volatile contamination.
Fire point
Temperature at which vapour supports sustained burning under the test conditions.
Helps assess fire risk during high-temperature operation.

blocks.text: Flash gives momentary ignition; fire point requires sustained burning and is normally higher. Adequately high values are desirable for hot service.

rows: Cloud point
Temperature at which oil first becomes cloudy on cooling due to wax separation.
Indicates wax deposition and possible filter blockage in cold service.
Pour point
Lowest temperature at which oil flows under the specified test conditions.
A low pour point is needed for cold starting and pumpability.

blocks.text: Cloud point marks the start of wax separation; pour point describes the low-temperature flow limit. Low values favour cold starting and pumpability.

rows: Flash point
Lowest specified-test temperature at which oil vapour ignites momentarily when a test flame is applied.
Indicates volatility and fire hazard; must be adequately above normal operating temperature.
Fire point
Temperature at which the ignited vapour sustains burning under the specified test conditions.
Indicates tendency to support continued combustion; normally higher than flash point.

blocks.text: Low values may indicate volatile contamination. High values are desirable for high-temperature use, but they do not alone establish overall lubricant quality or a safe operating limit.
Biodegradable lubricants break down by biological action under suitable conditions. Examples include suitably formulated vegetable-oil lubricants and biodegradable synthetic esters.

blocks.title: Advantages over conventional mineral-oil lubricants
items: Lower persistence after accidental release, reducing long-term environmental contamination.
Often derived partly from renewable feedstocks, such as vegetable oils.
Suitable formulations offer good lubricity and can reduce friction and wear.
Useful in agriculture, forestry, marine and other environmentally sensitive applications.

blocks.text: Biodegradability does not automatically mean non-toxic or superior in every property. Oxidation stability, cold-flow behaviour, hydrolytic stability and compatibility must be checked; appropriate additives/formulation may be required.
